title: What tyres will the teams have for the Mexico City GP?
excerpt:
The F1 paddock moves onto Mexico City for Round 19 of the 2026 season, with the drivers set to take on the breathtaking Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez – and tyre suppliers Pirelli have confirmed the compounds that will be in use throughout the weekend.

For this year's event the C3 has been selected as the hard compound, with the C4 as the medium and C5 as the soft. This marks a different choice from last year, when a compound step was attempted with the C2 as hard.

Drivers will get two sets of the hard tyre (marked white), three sets of the medium tyre (marked yellow), and eight sets of the soft tyre (marked red), as well as access to the green intermediate tyre and the blue full wets, should they be required.

An extra set of softs is reserved for those who reach Q3 in Qualifying, while all drivers must use at least two different slick compounds during the race, providing the track is dry.

"The main novelty for the weekend is the resurfacing of a large portion of the circuit, reads Pirelli's weekend preview. "The work covered the section from Turn 16 to Turn 1 and the stretch from Turn 7 to Turn 16, leaving only the first sector largely unchanged. New asphalt is normally associated with higher grip levels and lower roughness compared to an older surface. However, it will be important to assess its actual characteristics during the opening stages of the weekend.

"The Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez has traditionally been one of the least demanding circuits on tyres. Its many low-speed corners and limited lateral loads tend to keep wear under control. At the same time, the thin air reduces the aerodynamic load generated by the cars, increasing tyre slip and making graining a factor to watch closely. With a new and smoother asphalt surface, this characteristic could play an even more significant role in shaping strategy.

"In Mexico, the track is often quite dirty during the first sessions, with grip improving significantly lap after lap. This year, that evolution could be even more pronounced given the extensive resurfacing work.

"From a strategic point of view, the circuit’s low severity and the behaviour of the three compounds on tracks with similar characteristics could favour a one-stop race. Tyre management to extend stints will nevertheless remain an important factor, particularly considering that the rear axle is the most heavily stressed.

"The difference between the various strategic options may depend more on the confidence a driver can extract from a particular compound than on any genuine tyre life limitation. As seen at several events this season, some teams may be more inclined towards the softer compounds in order to benefit from the additional grip available, while others may favour the consistency and stability offered by the Hard.

"In any case, the Soft could once again play a central role. The C5 has demonstrated strong characteristics on low-severity circuits and could prove an attractive option not only in qualifying but also in the race, broadening the range of strategic possibilities compared to previous seasons.

"Another aspect to monitor will be braking performance. The altitude reduces aerodynamic efficiency and can make the management of the heaviest braking zones more challenging. The long main straight leading into Turn 1 could increase the risk of lock-ups, especially during the early stages of the weekend when grip levels are still limited."

For more information about Pirelli’s F1 tyres, visit pirelli.com.

title: What is the weather forecast for the Mexico City GP?
excerpt:
Mexico City is the next stop for the Formula 1 circus, the middle part of a triple-header that started in Austin and will conclude in Sao Paulo. But what kind of weather conditions will the drivers and teams be contending with this weekend?

Last year the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez dished up a warm and sunny race, with Lando Norris charging to victory on his way to his maiden Drivers' title. He beat Charles Leclerc and Max Verstappen as his team mate suffered a further blow to his championship hopes, Oscar Piastri finishing just fifth.

Norris might be hard pushed to repeat that victory, with McLaren struggling last weekend in Austin. Instead it will be all eyes on Kimi Antonelli, who could seal the title himself this weekend, with George Russell and Lewis Hamilton the two tasked with stopping the Italian.

Scroll down for a more detailed look at the forecast for the Mexico City Grand Prix.

title: 5 storylines we're excited about ahead of the Mexico City GP
excerpt:
From one huge event in Austin to another in Mexico, the action continues thick and fast as Kimi Antonelli moves closer to wrapping up the title. Aside from championship permutations, there’s plenty more to look forward to as we prepare for our latest visit to the fiesta that awaits in Mexico City.

Antonelli on the verge of the championship

It was so nearly a crowning weekend for Kimi Antonelli in Austin but he will get another chance to seal the deal and become the youngest World Champion just seven days later.

Victory in the United Sates Grand Prix opened the door for Antonelli to become champion, but Lewis Hamilton (fourth) and George Russell (eighth) each finished just one position higher than the Mercedes driver had needed them to be, ensuring the celebrations would have to wait for at least a week.

The equation is far more simple for Antonelli now. A top-nine finish in Sunday’s race will confirm him as World Champion, and even if misfortune befalls him and he finishes tenth or lower, he will still be champion if neither Russell nor Hamilton win the race. Tenth will even be enough if it’s Hamilton who wins, with only a Russell victory in that scenario preventing a title party.

Red Bull moves level with McLaren

Max Verstappen might not have been able to make it three wins in a row in Austin, but he did extend his podium streak to six consecutive top three finishes, and if you go back to his first podium of the year – at round five in Canada – he has only failed to finish on the podium when he’s seen the chequered flag on one occasion.

That was in Barcelona, where Verstappen was fourth, and two of his three DNFs have come when he looked set for a podium, too. So it’s not as if Red Bull haven’t been competitive for some time, but the recent upturn in form to secure wins has allowed it to close in and now draw level with McLaren in the Teams’ standings.

The two teams have 355 points to their names, with Red Bull classified ahead by virtue of having more second-placed finishes. The form guide suggests Red Bull could pull clear in that battle, but McLaren showed flashes of really strong pace in Austin and will be looking to unlock more of it to try and respond in Mexico City.

Perez hits 300

Mexico City is always a big weekend for the home hero Sergio Perez, who enjoys enormous support when returning to race at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez.

This weekend will be particularly special as Perez is set to make his 300th start in Formula 1, and will get to celebrate in front of his home crowd. He’s kicking off the festivities with a show run in Mexico City on Wednesday, before taking to the track on Friday and looking to help Cadillac continue their development as the newest team on the grid.

Perez signs contract extension to remain at Cadillac

That challenge is one that has reinvigorated Perez after a year on the sidelines, and he’ll be keen to help them move forward as quickly as possible. But it was always going to be a long-term project, and fans will be aware that simply reaching Q2 would be a huge achievement for Cadillac.

However he fares, Perez can expect enormous backing, and will look to give his supporters something to cheer for off-track if not on it, as he has agreed a contract extension to remain with Cadillac until at least 2029 and further extend that number of starts.

Rookie FP1 outings

Ever since it became mandatory for teams to run a rookie during FP1 sessions at some stage of the season, Mexico City has been one of the venues that has seen multiple appearances for drivers gaining experience in F1 machinery.

One of the most notable outings was for Ollie Bearman at Haas in 2023, catching the eye to such an extent that he was soon viewed as a certainty for a future race seat with the team.

Two new rookies will make their FP1 debuts, with Racing Bulls fielding F2 race winner Nikola Tsolov and F3 runner-up Freddie Slater appearing for Audi. They join a host of young drivers getting track time in Mexico City, as the likes of Fred Vesti, Leonardo Fornaroli, Jak Crawford, Luke Browning and Colton Herta will also continue their development with appearances for Mercedes, McLaren, Aston Martin, Williams and Cadillac respectively.

Red Bull junior Tsolov arrives in the midst of a tight battle with new Haas recruit Rafael Camara for the F2 crown, while Slater narrowly missed out on this season’s F3 title to Ugo Ugochukwu.

A unique test in front of a special crowd

I wrote the sentence “Almost every race weekend can be classified as a big event given the number of sellout crowds seen this season”, and fresh from a record 467,000 weekend attendance at Circuit of the Americas, the same point holds true as we head to Mexico.

The atmosphere at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez is always special, whether Sergio Perez is racing or not. Last year was a weekend where Perez was not on track and yet it was still a fiesta, particularly in the Foro Sol section where the track winds its way through an old baseball stadium, and the podium is located in front of an enormous crowd.

But when we talk about atmosphere, it’s not just related to the noise being made by the fans. The atmospheric conditions are also significant, with the Mexico City track the highest on the calendar at 2,200 metres above sea level.

Given Interlagos is next on the list at 800m, it shows the scale of the test for teams to handle the cooling challenges of racing at such altitude, while the aerodynamic devices on the cars themselves also offer far lower levels of downforce given the density of the air.

It’s most easily summed up by describing it as a weekend where you run Monaco levels of downforce but the car reacts as if you’re running a Monza-specific package, and it can lead to some eye-catching performances if certain teams find their cars suit the conditions better than others.

title: How F1 drivers and strategists tackle the Mexico City Grand Prix
excerpt:
Every race demands risk for reward, but for the Mexico City Grand Prix, at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, everything tends to be a little more extreme. It’s a race that breaks engines, fries brakes, breaks the spirit, and has a regular rotation of Safety Cars, VSCs and red flags to turn races on the simple caprices of fate – and all in front of the loudest, most raucous crowd in F1.

It can also be a race of subtle strategy, where overtaking is difficult. One-stop races tend to dominate, but nuances within those single-stops can make all the difference. It’s never dull in Mexico.

So how will the teams, drivers and strategists approach the weekend? It’s time to take a look in The Risk Perspective, in partnership with Marsh, Formula 1's Official Risk Partner and Official Insurance Brokering Partner.

The Set-Up

Altitude, altitude, altitude. Everything that happens around the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez is predicated on the circuit being at 2,250m above sea-level. It’s a monster, poking up out of the atmosphere, three-times the altitude of Interlagos, next on the list at 800m.

There’s a 20%-ish drop in air density, compared to sea-level, and so a corresponding 20% drop in downforce and cooling potential. The turbo engines don’t lose power like the old normally-aspirated engines did – but the turbo has to work a lot harder to deliver enough air, and this therefore tends to be an attrition race.

For cooling, the cars will all run with big brake scoops, and loose bodywork. Look closely at the sidepods and you’ll see a lot more shoulder louvres than are normally present. Look closely at the rear of the cars and you’ll see a lot more space between bodywork and powertrain – allowing for more airflow.

It creates a more draggy car, with the teams very keen to make sure they have enough cooling, but not a scrap more than is absolutely necessary.

Teams will run with all the downforce they can possibly find. In years past, the rule of thumb has been that Monaco levels of bodywork will deliver Monza levels of downforce – but since the advent of active aero, teams were able this year to run quite large wings in Monza, which means the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez will have by far the lowest downforce levels of the year, despite having the largest wings and every winglet and gurney the teams can find glued to the car.

The drop in downforce means the teams can set-up their cars to run a little lower for a given stiffness – though there’s always a lot of work to do figuring out how to set-up the cars in heave and roll to cope with the bumps and the kerbs the cars need to run.

5 storylines we're excited about ahead of the Mexico City GP

The Strategy: Charles-Antoine Florentin, Head of Race Strategy, Williams

“The biggest trap in Mexico is overreacting to Friday. The track starts very green and rubbers-in a lot over the weekend. The degradation often reduces drastically from free practice to the race. You’re always correcting practice data for track evolution, and the question is, by how much?

“Across practice we want to know four things: what are the real lap-time gaps between the three compounds? Can the soft tyre do a meaningful race stint? How much will the track improve by Sunday? How will the power unit cope with the altitude, where turbo speed and cooling are both harder?

“Regarding risks with set-up, most weekends, our main contribution as a strategy group is typically a steer on the trade-off between qualifying pace and race pace. Mexico is different, and we get more involved. Because of the altitude, everything cools less well: brakes, power unit, and now a bigger electrical system.

“The turbo also has to work harder in the thin air. You fix the cooling level before the race, and more cooling means more drag. How much you need depends on how long the car spends behind other cars, because running in someone’s wake increases overheating.

“So, we predict how much traffic each car will be in, and in which phase of the race. A car stuck in a train in the first stint is a different problem from one in traffic after the stops. That prediction feeds the cooling choice. Get it wrong one way and you give away performance. Get it wrong the other way and the driver has to manage temperatures, which costs time and makes them easy to pass.

“The straight is long, but the thin air takes away a lot of the tow. The harder part is getting close in the first place. The fast esses of the middle sector, and the stadium section, are sensitive to dirty air, so the following car loses ground before it reaches the straight.

“Teams' overtaking models puts numbers on that. For 2026, DRS is gone, and the car behind gets help from extra electrical energy instead. In Mexico, with the very long straight, teams and drivers will be sure to deploy as much energy as possible into T1, which will remain the prime overtaking corner.

“Regarding tyre choices, 2024 and 2025 had different tyre allocations. In 2024, the hard was the C3. In 2025, Pirelli skipped a step and brought the C2. This meant the lap-time difference between medium and hard was much higher than it was in 2024. That’s a penalty to carry for about 40 laps.

“Another big change was the tyres themselves. The 2025 tyres were much more resistant to graining and overheating. Those are normally what limit you in Mexico, because the thin air means low downforce and a lot of sliding. In Mexico, the soft degradation in 2025 was half what it was expected to be in 2024. This is why nobody wanted to race it in 2024.

“Because soft was the fastest tyre and could do half the race at low degradation, soft>medium became the natural one-stop in 2025, and soft-medium-soft a genuine alternative. Overall, 60% of the field stopped once and 40 % twice, last year.

“Some of this learning carries over in the 2026. The 2026 tyres behave more like the 2025 tyres than those of 2024, so graining and overheating could be less of a problem than they used to be here.

“Degradation is a bit higher than last year, though. The selection is also back to consecutive compounds, C3-C4-C5, so the hard could be much closer to the medium than last year’s C2. That brings medium>hard back into play – but the soft will still be a race tyre.

“We also plan for interruptions. Mexico has always seen at least a Safety Car or a Virtual Safety Car intervention.”

The Drivers’ Perspective: Sergio Perez

Happenstance means Sergio Perez celebrates his 300th Grand Prix start this weekend at his home Grand Prix. This moves the Cadillac driver above Sebastian Vettel to seventh outright on the list of F1 starts – not that the race wasn’t going to be special for Checo without the milestone.

Some 150,000 fans will be crammed into the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on Sunday, and they’ll all be chanting the same name. It makes the spine tingle even if you’re not Sergio Perez.

“Really how much has to happen that you make your 300th race at your home? It's incredible!” says Checo. “To have all the people that have been with me since day one, supporting me, all my sponsors, all my family, all my fans, it’s very special.

“We talk about it a lot, but the big thing here really is the altitude. It plays a massive part. It puts a lot of stress on the tyres, on the brakes, on the engine: everything is running to the absolute limit.

“From the driver’s perspective, the thing you really have to concentrate on is minimising the sliding. The downforce is very low, so that’s difficult, but it’s really, really key to getting a good lap, getting into a good rhythm. It’s super-critical.”

The key section: The Foro Sol

That the Foro Sol baseball stadium even exists was disheartening for many F1 fans, as it was constructed squarely in the path of the fearsome Curva Peraltada, the signature 180° banked corner that flings cars back onto the main straight, mixing high-speeds and incredible danger in the first two incarnations of the Mexican Grand Prix.

The section of track, from Turn 12 through to Turn 16, cuts through the stadium now, before returning for a half-Peraltada Turn 17, now named in honour of Nigel Mansell.

The stadium section itself is spectacular: a cauldron of noise looming over the track, where a low-speed sequence of corners rolls across what is usually the baseball diamond. This section is key to the lap because, as is usually the case, there’s much more time to be gained and lost in low speed – and more so at altitude where the cars aren’t quite so glued to the track as they would be with the downforce piled-on at sea-level.

This is particularly true on a Qualifying lap where the trick is ensuring the car arrives in the stadium with some life left in its tyres. Overheating the tyres earlier in the lap can cause real problems in the stadium, so there’s a need to judge carefully how hard to push.

The Greatest Race: 1968: A three-way title showdown

The stars aligned in 1968, with the final race of the year, at the future Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez (then the Magdalena Mixhuca Circuit) being the scene for a championship showdown between reigning World Champion Denny Hulme, of McLaren, 1962 Champion Graham Hill of Lotus, and future triple World Champion Jackie Stewart of Matra.

Hill led on 39 points, Stewart had 36, Hulme 33. There were nine points for victory, but with unreliability common, the title was there for the taking.

There was time to savour the title fight, with the race moved back two weeks to clear the decks for the Mexico City Summer Olympics. When F1 did finally arrive, it was Hill’s team mate Jo Siffert on pole, with Hill and Hulme third and fourth on the grid, with Stewart down in P7 – though starting position in the 1960s rarely had much bearing on the race result.

Hill made a fast start and took the lead, only to be passed by John Surtees who made a better one from P6. Hill came back and retook the lead before the end of the lap. Jackie Stewart also got a rocket and was up to P2, on the tail of his former BRM team mate by Lap 2.

The race refused to settle. Stewart took the lead on Lap 5; and Hulme made his way through the pack to be running P3, so the three contenders were holding the top three places. Siffert then started to recover from his start and passed Hulme; Hill retook the lead on Lap 10, before Hulme retired with a rear suspension failure.

It wasn’t quite a straight fight then between Hill and Stewart, as Siffert passed the Scotsman on Lap 17 and provided his Lotus team mate with something of a buffer… though Siffert was intent on victory and look the lead from his team mate on Lap 22.

He then suffered a broken throttle cable and was out of the race. It was then a straight fight between Hill and Stewart. Were Stewart to win, the pair would be level on points and Stewart would take the title.

They ran 1-2 for 25 laps, but just when the crowd might have been anticipating a grandstand finish, Stewart began to drop back, a fuel feed problem ending his challenge. He eventually finished seventh, lapped by Hill, who became a double World Champion, and Stewart would have to wait another year to open his account.

The Strategic Masterstroke: 2023 – Lando’s Massive Offset

2023 was the year McLaren returned from a decade in the wilderness to be a serious contender again. They notched-up nine podium finishes, four front row starts, and a Sprint victory. None of those things happened in Mexico, where they finished fifth and eighth.

Nevertheless, Team Principal Andrea Stella felt compelled post-race to call it “one of the best races I have been part of,” thanks to an oddball strategy that had Lando Norris charge from 17th on the grid to fifth at the flag.

It didn’t look so clever on Saturday, when Norris was ejected in Q1, having made a mistake on one attempt, having a car issue on another, and seeing a third attempt banjaxed by a yellow flag. The car had pace, but overtaking is difficult at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez.

While the straight is very long, the lack of downforce made the impact of DRS negligible. A car has to be very close coming onto the straight – but again, the lack of load makes them very twitchy when following closely through the high-speed final corner. McLaren’s strategy for Norris therefore, was to keep him away from other cars unless he had a sizeable tyre advantage.

And so, when the tyre blankets came off on the grid, Norris was the only driver with a soft tyre fitted. He used that to claim three places in the opening laps, before making an early pit stop, for hards. That dropped him back to P18 – but gave him 17 seconds of clear air up to Esteban Ocon.

McLaren, however, were giving him lap times for Nico Hulkenberg, running in P8, confident he could undercut his way up to the German… which he did.

Norris passed Ocon, Fernando Alonso, Lance Stroll, Valtteri Bottas and Alex Albon on track, but made up five more places with the undercut, to be running P8 on Lap 33, when a Safety Car came out, following a heavy crash for Kevin Magnussen.

This wasn’t what Lando needed, because it was too early to ditch the hard compound, but he came into the pits anyway, because a new set would be less of a problem than restarting the old hard tyre.

As soon as he committed to that, everything went wrong. First of all the Safety Car turned into a red flag, and then at the restart, Lando had a poor getaway that dropped him to P14. After that it was all about patience.

The medium tyre he had for the final stint had a tendency to overheat, so the team had him play a very long game – targeting George Russell in P5, but asking Norris to use all of the race to get there. He picked off a car every few laps: Bottas on 41; Gasly, Ocon and Hulkenberg as a job-lot on 45,46,47; Albon on 49.

Piastri moved aside on 56; Ricciardo fell on 60, and then Norris took seven laps to cruise-up behind the Mercedes of Russell. Russell defended hard, but Norris had tyres in good shape, brakes that were cool and a battery pack fully charged. He made his final overtake five laps from home.

The first half of a race was a tactical masterclass from McLaren’s strategists; the second half proved out the adage that there’s no strategy as effective as having a fast car. It did, however, demonstrate that you do have to use that fast car wisely.

title: Perez signs Cadillac contract extension until at least 2029
excerpt:
Sergio Perez has extended his contract with the Cadillac Formula 1 Team, ensuring the Mexican driver will remain with the American outfit until at least 2029.

Cadillac announced on Wednesday ahead of the Mexico City Grand Prix that they had retained the services of Perez, who joined the project ahead of the team’s F1 debut in 2026.

“Joining Cadillac Formula 1 Team from day one was a project I truly believed in, and extending my commitment feels like a natural continuation of this chapter,” said Perez.

“Building a Formula 1 team from the ground up takes time, relentless work and patience, but the progress we are making together is incredibly rewarding. There is still a lot of work ahead of us and I am fully committed for the next three years.

“I want to thank Dan (Towriss), Mark (Reuss), and everyone at TWG Motorsports and General Motors for the opportunity to build on what we have started together.

ANALYSIS: Why Cadillac moved quickly to secure Perez’s F1 future

"To every member of this special team, at the track, in the US, the UK, and our fans, thank you for your support and trust. I won’t let you down. Let’s keep pushing!”

Perez has taken six Grand Prix wins during a career that has included spells at Sauber, McLaren, Force India, Racing Point and Red Bull, and will make his 300th F1 start in front of his home fans this weekend in Mexico City.

Although Perez and Cadillac have yet to score a point this season, the team have steadily improved over the course of the 2026 campaign as they look to move further up the grid.

“On the eve of a special weekend in Mexico City, we’re thrilled to announce that Checo will remain an integral part of Cadillac Formula 1 Team for years to come,” said Dan Towriss, CEO, Cadillac Formula 1 Team.

“Building a competitive team in F1 is a long-term journey, and securing Checo’s talent and leadership gives us the continuity and commitment we need to build on the strong foundation established in our first year.

"Together, we are focused on the next phase of our journey, pushing the team forward and making progress up the grid.”

title: Formula 1 publishes first sport-wide Social Impact Report
excerpt:
Formula 1 has today published its first sport-wide Social Impact Report, revealing that more than 500,000 young people across 71 countries accessed and benefitted from Formula 1 programmes designed to educate, inspire and open pathways into the sport in 2025.

Alongside the report, Formula 1 has renewed its flagship Engineering Scholarship for a further three academic years, committing more than £2.4 million in funding. Founded in 2021, the scholarship programme addresses some of the key barriers to higher education for these students including the financial burden and accessing opportunities and has supported 48 students to date.

The programme covers full tuition fees and living costs for students from underrepresented backgrounds, giving them unrivalled access to Formula 1 through placements with F1 teams, exposure to the world-class technology behind the fastest cars in motorsport, exclusive visits to the Formula 1 Media and Technology Centre, and behind-the-scenes experiences at Grand Prix weekends.

Ten new scholars will join each year from 2026/27 to 2028/29, studying at the University of Strathclyde, Imperial College London, the University of Cambridge, the University of Oxford, and MUNER in Italy.

The report brings together, for the first time, the collective contribution of Formula 1, the FIA, all 10 teams and 24 race promoters during the 2025 season. It marks an important milestone in the sport’s efforts and on the recommendations of The Hamilton Commission, launched by Sir Lewis Hamilton and the Royal Academy of Engineering in 2021, and follows the publication of the sport’s first Diversity and Inclusion Charter, signed by Formula 1, the FIA and all 10 teams in 2024 (the Cadillac F1 Team signed the charter from the 2026 season, when they entered the sport).

Together, the report and scholarship renewal demonstrate how the sport is working to create opportunities for underrepresented groups, inspire future talent and make motorsport more accessible to all.

With 24 races across 21 countries, a fanbase of more than 830 million people and a cumulative annual television audience of 1.7 billion, Formula 1 is uniquely positioned to inspire future generations and broaden access to opportunities within motorsport. Initiatives such as the British Council’s Learning Sectors education programme, which has worked with more than 150,000 students across four countries in STEM learning, promoter-led community activities delivered at all 24 Grands Prix, and charitable fundraising efforts all help to achieve this ambition.

2025 highlights include:

500,000+ young people given access to the sport through education, STEM and inspiration programmes globally

100% of Diversity and Inclusion Charter signatories delivering social impact programmes

1,000+ skills and talent development opportunities spotlighting motorsport and related industries

10 students awarded the Formula 1 Engineering Scholarship in 2025, taking the total supported since the scheme launched in 2021 to 48

£2.4 million committed to renew the Formula 1 Engineering Scholarship until at least 2028/29, supporting 10 new students each year with tuition fees and living expenses

29,000+ schools compete annually in the STEM Racing global education initiative

700+ schools across the UK, South Africa, India and Brazil participated in the British Council’s Learning Sectors education programme

€100,000 donations given to four organisations awarded the F1 Allwyn Global Community Award

2,500+ young people participating in activities delivered at Formula 1 events

50+ wishes granted through Formula 1's partnership with Make-A-Wish

140 young people attended F1 Academy workshops

Formula 1 will continue to expand programmes highlighted in the report, including Learning Sectors and the F1 Allwyn Global Community Award, reaching more children and communities around the world. The sport will strengthen its approach to governance, measurement and reporting to better understand results, share progress and maximise the long-term value of its social impact work.

Stefano Domenicali, President and CEO of Formula 1, said: “Formula 1 has an extraordinary power to inspire, and we want everyone to believe there is a place for them in our sport. We are turning our commitments into action, working across motorsport to break down barriers and widen access for future generations.

“We are proud of the progress made and grateful for the collective efforts of Lewis Hamilton, the Hamilton Commission, the FIA, our teams, race promoters, partners and the many organisations helping to create lasting change. By renewing the Formula 1 Engineering Scholarship for a further three academic years and investing in young people and communities, we will open more doors, nurture talent and inspire the next generation to believe that a future in Formula 1 is within their reach.”

title: Liam Lawson dilemma amplifies Racing Bulls' identity crisis
excerpt:
Racing Bulls has the good problem of three viable drivers for two F1 seats, but what Red Bull does with Liam Lawson will be symbolic of a larger struggle.

28 October 8:00PM

Red Bull has a Liam Lawson problem.

Lawson, as I have said so many times this year, has been one of the standout performers in F1 this season. That should not, and cannot, be understated. In fact, you start to run out of ways to do his results justice; to fairly describe how impressive he's been.

The Racing Bulls driver is comfortably best of the rest behind the top four teams. Even if you take out his three rounds deputising for the injured Isack Hadjar at Red Bull, he is still a country mile clear of Alpine's Pierre Gasly in the hunt for ninth in the drivers' standings.

On 77 points to the Frenchman's 42, 14 of that haul was earned behind the wheel of the RB22, meaning 63 were claimed in the usual cockpit of his VCARB 03, outpacing Gasly at a clip of three to two — in three fewer rounds, no less.

Those grands prix alongside Max Verstappen have done his prospects no harm at all. Even if they did not secure his future at Racing Bulls, you'd think they guarantee him a future in F1 in some way, shape or form.

He might argue it wasn't vindication or redemption, that there were no wrongs to right from his brief tenure at Red Bull in 2025, but when the chips were down, and the stakes were at their highest, Lawson stood up and demanded he be counted. Consider that particular demon vanquished.

I can't stand the word 'deserves' when it comes to sport. You don't deserve anything; sometimes the best wins, sometimes they don't. But you do earn things, and Lawson has done all he can and more to earn his place on the grid next term.

So, full disclosure, if I were a decision-maker at Red Bull, I'd have re-signed him to a new contract yesterday.

And therein lies the issue for the top brass at the energy drinks manufacturer's racing team: Lawson wasn't meant to be performing this well. At least, according to the designs of the old Racing Bulls.

The internal struggle

But new era, new requirements, and that is what the team must grapple with.

Because, underneath the immediate call on whether to retain Lawson for next season, Racing Bulls must decide what type of team it wants to be moving forward, and its driver line-up is emblematic of that.

Since purchasing the team from Minardi and becoming Toro Rosso in 2006, the Faenza-based squad has evolved through various guises to become the pithy and undeniably catchy Visa Cash App Racing Bulls — or just Racing Bulls to you and me — it is today.

That is not the identity crisis I speak of. Because I, like so few, kind of love the sheer audacity of the team's full name. It plays into the effervescent charm of a team that doesn't take itself too seriously — and it's great for sponsorship...

Racing Bulls is playful, fun, incontrovertibly cool, and finds a deep and delightful passion in ragebaiting (poking fun at to the non-Gen Z amongst us) its two drivers — the poor, now not-so-unsuspecting Lawson and rookie team-mate Arvid Lindblad — for social media likes.

There is an ease to all the team is and represents. But it has a decidedly not-easy dilemma on its hands: keep Lawson for 2027, or promote highly-touted junior driver Nikola Tsolov?

[Article continues below]

A larger question to answer

Now, the part Racing Bulls would probably like me to write is that neither of its two race seats has been officially confirmed yet, so it isn't strictly a Lawson vs. Tsolov scenario.

In reality, it has three really good options for just two seats. However, for all intents and purposes, it is being read as advertised, because Lindblad has strung together an eye-catching rookie season and is just 19 years of age, meaning he has bags of potential and plenty of time — and room — to grow.

Lawson, on the other hand, is basically Jurassic at 24 years old. And this tension typifies the internal struggle: What sort of team does Racing Bulls want to be?

Choosing Tsolov over Lawson wouldn't, in itself, contradict the argument that Racing Bulls is its own team, but it cuts to the heart of a larger question.

Does it wish to be a farm for emerging talent, all with the sole aim of producing a driver who may emulate the great achievements of Sebastian Vettel and Verstappen, one that casts aside talented drivers when it becomes apparent they fall short of that admittedly sky-high standard?

Or does Racing Bulls also desire to be a legitimate entity in its own right, stepping out of the shadow of its big sister with its own values and identity?

Because of the so-called B-team structure, it will likely never compete for consistent wins and championships. Doing so would be superfluous given that Red Bull exists. But that doesn't make Racing Bulls redundant. The team could aspire to be the best of the rest, as it and Lawson undoubtedly are this season, in addition to having its own personality.

Helmut Marko, the architect and champion of the team's ruthless and unforgiving farm system, weighed in last week, arguing that by the old way of doing things, Lawson's Racing Bulls seat should go to Tsolov. I'm sure that was viewed as particularly helpful.

Much of what Red Bull boss Laurent Mekies said when he was at the helm of the second team, and what CEO Peter Bayer and current team principal Alan Permane continue to say on the matter, points to a Racing Bulls that is unapologetically itself and has a core purpose beyond only developing talent for its sister operation, which it just so happens to be owned by, even if it is an important aspect.

If it is more than just a mere proving ground and a stepping stone to Red Bull, now is the time to prove that.

For if that truly is the case, by extension of that logic, there should be no qualms in extending Lawson's stay. Because, as already stressed, he has more than earned it.

title: Daniel Ricciardo reflects on F1 exit 'humiliation' with surprise Red Bull stance
excerpt:
Daniel Ricciardo has opened up on how he coped with his exit from F1 two years ago.

Following the Singapore Grand Prix in 2024, Racing Bulls confirmed that Liam Lawson would replace Ricciardo for the remainder of the campaign.

It marked Ricciardo's last race as an F1 driver, bringing an end to his 13-year stint in the sport that saw him win eight grands prix.

Ricciardo slipped away from public view after his departure and returned home to Australia to attend to personal matters he had little time for while navigating the F1 schedule.

However, the 37-year-old admitted he struggled to come to terms with the reality of the situation.

"The first phase straight after Singapore, it was still trying to stay tall and strong," Ricciardo told the Beyond the Grid podcast.

"It's like a coping mechanism, or trying to outwardly project that I'm fine, it's all good, ultimately hiding from a feeling of humiliation.

"That was the first phase of just thinking everything was okay. But obviously, I was very, very hurt inside."

[Article continues below]

Ricciardo grateful Red Bull 'pulled the trigger' on F1 career

Ricciardo's most successful stint in F1 came during his time at Red Bull from 2014 to 2018.

High-reaching results were much harder to come by after he left the team, and he went through a particularly difficult period with McLaren before his final stint with the Red Bull sister squad.

The Australian admitted he feels grateful that Red Bull made the decision for him, to save him from further agony.

"I can tell you right now, in Monaco, 2022, after the race, I'm sitting in my apartment talking to my team, and I was like, 'I don't want to do this anymore'.

"There are moments where I've wanted to just get away from it, but the reality is, you have people around you that tell you 'you're great, you can still do it'.

"You end up also believing a lot of these voices. I know they don't mean harm, but you don't really get a chance to have your own thoughts much.

"I still don't like how it ended, but there's also a part of me which is grateful that they pulled the trigger.

"I wouldn't want to be doing it now."

title: Nikola Tsolov replaces Liam Lawson at Racing Bulls for Mexico FP1
excerpt:
Racing Bulls has confirmed that Nikola Tsolov will take over Liam Lawson's VCARB 03 for the first free practice session of the Mexico City Grand Prix, marking the Bulgarian's maiden appearance in an official F1 session.

The session at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez represents a significant step for the Red Bull Junior Programme driver, who joined the scheme in 2025 after winning the Spanish F4 Championship in 2022 and finishing runner-up in FIA Formula 3 this year.

Tsolov arrives in Mexico on the back of a maiden Formula 1 test with the team at Imola in August, where he covered 690 kilometres across 143 laps in the 2025-specification VCARB 02, powered by the Honda RBPTH003 engine, as part of a Testing of Previous Cars programme.

He currently competes for Campos Racing in Formula 2, where he sits second in the standings, seven points behind leader Rafael Câmara with two rounds remaining. His campaign has included six wins, among them victories in Melbourne and Miami and a sweep of both races at Silverstone.

"A big thank you to VCARB for giving me this opportunity in Mexico. Following my test with the team at Imola in August, I'm excited to take this next step, build on that experience and learn more about the car and the current regulations. I'll focus on making the most of the session, working closely with the team and providing useful feedback," Tsolov said.

Under the 2026 sporting regulations, every competitor must field an eligible rookie, defined as a driver with no more than two Grand Prix starts, in at least two free practice sessions per car across the season, amounting to four mandatory rookie outings per team. Sunday's running in Mexico goes some way to fulfilling that requirement for Racing Bulls.

Racing Bulls team principal Alan Permane said: "Running Nikola in FP1 is an important step in his development within the Red Bull Junior Programme.

"It reflects our commitment to nurturing emerging talent and giving our junior drivers valuable track time and the support they need to learn and develop.

"Having already worked with Nikola at Imola, we're looking forward to seeing him build on that experience in Mexico and to the feedback he can provide to help support our preparations for the weekend."

title: Sergio Perez to join rarefied F1 club in historic Mexican GP
excerpt:
Sergio Perez is to become just the seventh F1 driver in history to achieve 300 grand prix starts during his home race in Mexico City this weekend.

Perez currently has 299 starts to his name and will reach his triple-century at his home track, becoming the first driver to reach such a milestone in front of his home crowd.

The Mexican is to follow Fernando Alonso, Lewis Hamilton, Kimi Raikkonen, Rubens Barrichello, Michael Schumacher, and Jenson Button in starting 300 races, with Perez actually set to enter his 304th grand prix.

The so-called 'missing races' for Perez are the 2011 Monaco and Canadian GPs, where he withdrew following a qualifying accident in Monaco, the 2014 Malaysian GP, where a gearbox issue put him out; and the 2020 British GP, where he tested positive for COVID-19.

Sebastian Vettel has been entered into 300 grands prix, and actually started 300 grand prix formation laps, but has only completed 299 and a half of them after breaking down with engine failure on the way to the grid of the 2016 Bahrain GP.

Hamilton is also closing in on 400 grands prix, with Mexico City set to be his 399th entry and start. The only grand prix he has missed since his debut in 2007 was the 2020 Sakhir Grand Prix, after a positive COVID test - that race, of course, being won by Perez...

title: Why Ferrari keeps finding joy with upgrades despite exposing crucial weakness
excerpt:
Ferrari's final major aerodynamic upgrade of the F1 season delivered encouraging results in Austin. Still, the SF-26's progress has also underlined the importance of addressing its power unit deficit for 2027, explains RacingNews365 technical analyst Paolo Fillisetti.

Ferrari introduced its final major aerodynamic upgrade package of the season at the United States Grand Prix in Austin. However, the SF-26's performance in Texas should not be attributed solely to these latest developments.

Instead, the result reflected the cumulative effect of successive upgrades, each building on the improvements delivered by previous packages.

Indeed, it had become apparent early in the season that the SF-26 was a particularly receptive platform for technical development.

Every upgrade package introduced by Ferrari has delivered the expected gains, not simply because the aerodynamic solutions were effective, but also because the underlying car concept provided a sound foundation on which to build.

Throughout the season, the SF-26 has progressively addressed several of its initial weaknesses, including its tendency to generate excessive drag.

At the same time, Ferrari has broadened the car's operating window, allowing it to perform competitively across an increasingly diverse range of circuits.

[Article continues below]

Ferrari's development success puts power unit deficit in spotlight

The engineering team led by Loic Serra has successfully balanced aerodynamic requirements with the car's mechanical characteristics throughout this development process.

Crucially, the upgrades have also helped compensate for some of the limitations imposed by the Ferrari power unit, whose performance has remained a relative weakness.

As the chassis has improved, however, those engine limitations have become increasingly difficult to overlook.

Even rival engineers regard the SF-26 as a particularly successful design in terms of its chassis and suspension architecture. Consequently, the need to bring the power unit up to a comparable competitive level has become ever more apparent.

Importantly, Ferrari's power unit shortcomings are not the consequence of packaging compromises made to prioritise aerodynamic performance.

Instead, they stem from fundamental design decisions within the power unit itself.

One example is the adoption of a smaller-diameter turbine, a conceptual choice that has influenced engine performance independently of how the unit is installed in the chassis.

This distinction is significant because it indicates that the performance deficit cannot simply be resolved through changes to the car's aerodynamic packaging.

[Article continues below]

© XPB Images

Ferrari targeting fundamentally new power unit for 2027

Looking ahead to 2027, the power unit department led by Enrico Gualtieri has a clearly defined objective: to provide Ferrari's next challenger with an engine that does not suffer from the performance limitations of the current design.

Achieving that target will be far from straightforward, particularly given the extent of the changes required.

However, Ferrari now has a substantial body of performance data on which to base its development decisions, allowing its engineers to identify the areas requiring fundamental revision.

The resulting changes are expected to be sufficiently extensive that Ferrari's 2027 power unit will effectively represent an entirely new design.

With the SF-26 demonstrating the strength of Ferrari's chassis concept and its ability to respond consistently to aerodynamic development, the emphasis is increasingly shifting towards the engine department.

The challenge for 2027 will be to ensure that the power unit can finally match the potential of the rest of the car.

title: F1 champions vital cause with multi-million-pound investment and important report
excerpt:
Formula 1 has announced a £2.4 million investment in its Engineering Scholarship programme alongside the publication of its first sport-wide Social Impact Report, highlighting efforts to make motorsport more accessible to underrepresented groups.

The report reveals that more than 500,000 young people across 71 countries benefited from education, STEM and community outreach initiatives delivered throughout 2025.

The findings bring together the contributions of F1, the FIA, all 10 teams and 24 race promoters, demonstrating the sport's commitment to improving diversity and accessibility.

The initiatives also build on recommendations made by the Hamilton Commission, established by seven-time F1 drivers' champion Lewis Hamilton and the Royal Academy of Engineering in 2021.

F1 has committed more than £2.4 million to extend its Engineering Scholarship programme for another three academic years, through to 2028/29.

Launched in 2021, the initiative has supported 48 students from underrepresented backgrounds, covering tuition fees and living expenses while providing placements with F1 teams. A further 10 students will join annually over the next three years.

F1 president and CEO Stefano Domenicali said: "Formula 1 has an extraordinary power to inspire, and we want everyone to believe there is a place for them in our sport.

"We are turning our commitments into action, working across motorsport to break down barriers and widen access for future generations."

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem welcomed the findings and continued investment.

"Motorsport has the power to transform lives, and we have a responsibility to ensure its benefits reach beyond the racetrack," he said.

"Together, we are breaking down barriers, developing future talent and creating new pathways into our sport."

[Article continues below]

The report also highlights more than 1,000 skills and talent development opportunities, while over 29,000 schools participate annually in the STEM Racing initiative.

More than 150,000 students across four countries have also benefited from the British Council's Learning Sectors education programme.

F1's head of ESG, Ellen Jones, described the scholarship renewal as "offering sustained support that can remove financial barriers and help more students from underrepresented backgrounds take their first steps towards engineering careers".

UK skills minister Jacqui Smith MP also praised the initiative.

"Engineering is one of the industries most critical to our economic future, and we need more young people, from all backgrounds, to see it as a career for them," she said.

F1 intends to expand its existing programmes while strengthening how its impact is measured and reported.

title: 2026 F1 Mexican Grand Prix - Mexico City weather forecast
excerpt:
2026 F1 Mexican Grand Prix - Mexico City weather forecast

Teams arriving at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez this week can expect largely settled conditions across the Mexico City Grand Prix weekend, with only a brief rain threat on Friday afternoon.

Friday's opening practice session is forecast to bring temperatures of 21°C to 23°C, sunny intervals and a gentle northerly breeze, giving drivers a relatively comfortable first look at the high-altitude circuit.

Conditions are expected to warm slightly for FP2, with the mercury rising to 26°C, though a higher chance of rainfall is forecast compared with the rest of the weekend. Showers are considered unlikely to actually materialise, however, with the session expected to stay dry.

Saturday's build-up to qualifying looks cooler and calmer. FP3 is expected to see temperatures drop back to 20°C to 21°C, under sunny skies with a gentle northerly wind similar to Friday morning.

Qualifying itself is forecast to be a touch warmer at 25°C, still under sunny conditions, though with stronger wind than in final practice, albeit still within gentle limits.

Sunday's race is expected to take place in 24°C sunny conditions, with no rain in the forecast.

That should offer some reassurance to teams managing the unique demands of the 2,200-metre-plus altitude venue, where thinner air already reduces downforce and increases strain on cooling systems and turbochargers regardless of ambient temperature.

With Pirelli having nominated its softest three compounds, the C3, C4 and C5, for the round, stable and dry conditions throughout the weekend should allow teams to focus purely on managing degradation and graining rather than variable grip from changing weather.

title: Kimi Antonelli reveals if he will choose driver number '1' as F1 champion
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has revealed he will stick with the number '12' for 2027, even if he enters the year as the reigning champion.

Drivers who win the title are eligible to use number '1', as it is solely reserved for the driver who most recently topped the standings.

This year, it is being run by McLaren's Lando Norris, who clinched his maiden title at last year's Abu Dhabi Grand Prix.

The Briton took over the rights to the number from Max Verstappen, who had it attached to his Red Bull from 2022 to 2025 during his years as the reigning champion.

Antonelli enters this weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix with a high chance of securing the title, needing only ninth on the road on Sunday to become the sport's youngest ever champion.

He will then be able to choose his number for 2027, but the Italian has no interest in changing.

"First, I have to get the job done in Mexico. But I think that once that's done, I'll still be racing with number 12," Antonelli told Blick.

The only driver who previously passed up on the option to run number 1 as the champion since the introduction of the rule in 2014 was Lewis Hamilton, who retained '44' during his successful stint with Mercedes.

Antonelli has several reasons why the number 12 is so special to him. First, it's a tribute to his great idol: Ayrton Senna.

The Brazilian raced with that number between 1985 and 1988 and also won his first world title with it at McLaren.

In addition, 12 was also Antonelli's starting number when he made his debut in Formula 4, his first experience in a formula car. Furthermore, he was 12 years old when he was accepted into Mercedes' junior program.

title: Red Bull give first verdict on new Max Verstappen right-hand man
excerpt:
Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies has praised Tom Hart for his debut as Max Verstappen's race engineer in a "complicated" United States Grand Prix.

In the past, Simon Rennie has deputised for Gianpiero Lambiase in Verstappen's ear, but it was Hart who took over radio duties from 'GP', as he is affectionately known, at the Circuit of the Americas, as he gears up to assume the role full-time.

Lambiase is leaving the Milton Keynes-based team for McLaren imminently to become chief racing officer under Andrea Stella, so Red Bull has devised a plan to bed his replacement in.

Hart has worked at Red Bull since 2012 and has been closely involved with Verstappen's car since 2020 as a performance engineer.

To smooth the handover, the pair will split the remaining races between them. Hart will also be on the radio in São Paulo and Las Vegas, while Lambiase returns for Mexico City, Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

Verstappen finished third in Austin, behind pole-sitter Kimi Antonelli and Charles Leclerc, but Mekies was pleased with how Hart's debut went in an otherwise disappointing afternoon for the four-time F1 drivers' champion.

"Look, I think he did an excellent job," Mekies said of Hart, when speaking to media, including RacingNews365, after the race.

"You see me smiling, because I certainly remember what it is to be on your first race as a race engineer, and he picked a fairly complicated race to do that.

"That was not his choice – but jokes aside, I think he really did an excellent job."

[Article continues below]

Effusive praise for Hart

Expanding on his initial assessment, Mekies shared how well Hart handled the flow of information and communication between Verstappen and the rest of his performance team.

"First qualifying, first race, he has managed to channel very well the work of the engineering teams behind him to Max," he explained.

"Of course the race was a complicated race, and we are probably a bit frustrated with the P3, which is the good news, but I really think he did an excellent job, and he was very well supported by GP as well in the background.

"You cannot recreate a relationship in no time, but I have every confidence that we are going to see him ramping up and building that relationship with Max.

"As part of our plan, we will alternate Tom and GP to the end of the year. It's a combination of other considerations; it's what we do with FP1 drivers and so forth and so on. It’s just part of the plan."

title: Lewis Hamilton pinpoints where he lost out on 'awesome' Max Verstappen fight
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton believes his lack of pace in the first two stints in the United States GP cost him a shot at Max Verstappen's podium.

In the final stint, Hamilton had fresher tyres than Verstappen and was carving chunks of time out of the Red Bull on his hard compound rubber as he tried to steal away a podium finish.

Ultimately, Hamilton fell 1.020s short of passing the Dutchman, but his challenge was stunted by a late virtual safety car for Valtteri Bottas's stricken Cadillac.

Although the VSC gave Verstappen a lifeline and reduced the green flag laps Hamilton had to attack, the Ferrari driver felt that the lack of pace and understeer in his SF-26 in the first two stints had left him with too much to recover in his final charge back to fourth place - including a pass on Lando Norris.

"I think probably I would have got to have a little bit of a battle with Max maybe in the last couple of laps," Hamilton told media, including RacingNews365, when directly asked if the VSC had cost him a podium.

"That would have been awesome, but it was all the result of the first two stints [that I was behind].

"I just lost so much ground, and I can't be giving up that time in the future; I really feel happy with how I drove.

"But it just took two whole stints to try and get this car to turn, and then once it started to turn in the third stint, I was back on the pace with the cars ahead.

"It was 18 seconds to [race-winner Antonelli] ahead, and those guys were obviously very quick, so I've just got to work on that."

Second place fight heats up

Following the Austin race, the fight for the runner-up spot in the drivers' championship has closed up.

title: Lando Norris returns to F2 after clinching coveted entry
excerpt:
Formula 2 has confirmed the 11 teams that will make up the grid for the 2027 season, which includes Lando Norris' squad.

Earlier this year, Norris announced the formation of the LN4 Fusion team after taking over selected assets of AIX Racing, setting itself up for entries in various junior categories.

It was already confirmed that the team would partake in the Formula 3 championship, but its junior championship participation has now extended to F2, seen as the last stepping stone before F1.

As expected, LN4 Fusion takes over the entry previously held by AIX Racing, with no other new entries confirmed for the 2027-2029 cycle.

"We received strong interest from teams around the world for this new three-year cycle, underlining the strength and appeal of our Championship," said F2 CEO Bruno Michel.

"We have retained ten of our current teams, who have consistently demonstrated their commitment to providing the best possible environment for young drivers to prepare for Formula 1.

"I am also pleased to welcome LN4 Fusion to the grid.

"They will bring considerable expertise, and I am confident they will make a valuable contribution to the Championship."

LN4 Fusion will race under an Italian licence, but has not yet announced the two drivers that will form its line-up.

In F3, the squad has confirmed that James Egozi, Gabriel Gomez and Dion Gowda will occupy the seats.

title: Charles Leclerc voices Ferrari concern after identifying key victory-costing moment
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has declared that Ferrari is "not robust enough" over a full race weekend, identifying qualifying as the moment his hopes of winning the United States Grand Prix disappeared.

Leclerc started fourth at the Circuit of the Americas after a difficult Saturday but recovered to finish second, 13 seconds behind race winner Kimi Antonelli.

The Monegasque driver had topped the timesheets across the first two free practice sessions, and in Q2, only to see that pace evaporate when it mattered most in Q3, where he qualified fourth, two-and-a-half tenths of a second off Antonelli's pole time.

Victory returned to the conversation during the race itself, with Ferrari committing Leclerc to an aggressive two-stop strategy that exploited strong late pace on the hard compound.

It was enough for Leclerc to pass Max Verstappen in the closing stages and claim second, even as Antonelli's one-stop approach from pole kept him out of reach at the front.

Speaking in parc fermé, the Ferrari driver called it a satisfying result but one that fell short of the ultimate goal.

"It was quite a good race," he reflected after getting out of his car. "Unfortunately, we came short of the victory, which is eventually our target.

"But at the end of the day, it was a positive race. We had good pace. The first stint was a little bit more difficult. Kimi went for a one-stop, which was not really on our cards, to be honest.

"But we were in the race with Max, and we had good pace. It was a fun race, with quite nice battles at the start and then later on with Lando [Norris] and Max."

Later, in the post-race top three press conference, Leclerc pinpointed where the weekend went wrong, telling media, including RacingNews365, that Ferrari's qualifying struggles were the decisive factor.

"If you look at FP1, FP2 and FP3, we were very strong," Leclerc said. "If you look at qualifying, at the end of the day in Q3, it was extremely difficult to bring the tyres up to temperature, and we probably lost a shot at the victory there.

"Kimi was very strong, so, yeah, as a whole weekend, I think we're just not robust enough."
